lesson.title: Sorting DNA by Size: Reading the Bands
lesson.summary: Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size by pulling them through a porous gel with an electric field, with smaller fragments migrating farther than larger ones in a given amount of time.
lesson.body:
Once a restriction enzyme has cut a DNA sample into pieces, or once a technique like PCR has generated a DNA product, an obvious next question is whether the fragments are actually the size expected. Gel electrophoresis answers that question by physically sorting DNA fragments according to their length.

The technique relies on a simple physical fact: DNA's sugar-phosphate backbone carries a negative charge along its entire length, regardless of sequence. Samples are loaded into small wells cut into a slab of agarose, a gelatin-like, porous material, which is submerged in a buffer solution, and an electric field is applied across the gel with the positive electrode at the far end. Because DNA is negatively charged, every fragment migrates toward that positive electrode. The gel matrix itself acts like an obstacle course of microscopic pores: short DNA fragments wiggle through those pores relatively easily and travel farther in a given amount of time, while long fragments get slowed down much more and stay closer to the wells they started in. After running for a set period, the current is switched off, and the fragments have spread out into a series of distinct bands ordered by size.

To see the results, the gel is treated with a dye that binds DNA and glows under ultraviolet light, revealing the band pattern directly. Researchers routinely run a DNA ladder, a mixture of fragments of known, pre-determined sizes, in a lane alongside the experimental samples; since migration distance is directly related to fragment size, comparing an unknown band's position to the ladder gives a reliable estimate of that fragment's length.

Gel electrophoresis is the natural companion to the previous two sections: it is how scientists confirm that a restriction enzyme cut a DNA sample into the fragment sizes predicted by its recognition sites, and later sections will show it used just as routinely to check that a PCR reaction produced the correct product and that a cloning experiment worked as intended. Beyond the research lab, this same size-sorting principle underlies applications like forensic DNA fingerprinting and diagnostic tests for certain genetic conditions.
